seo.title: Karmic tail 9 21 3 compatibility: The Hermit, The World, The Empress
seo.description: Karmic tail 9 21 3 compatibility: solitude for two, a road across the whole world and the task of building a home, read through Stevenson and Fanny.

title: The 9-21-3 karmic tail in compatibility: a lighthouse above the door
short: The 9-21-3 karmic tail in compatibility belongs to a couple who share a lantern but for a long time have no shared home. The entry to the task is The Hermit: the two are happy on their own, with a quiet language of their own and a light only they know about. The middle of the task is The World: the couple carries that light along roads, through moves, across a whole world built for two. The main task is The Empress: to stop and grow something visible — a home, a garden, a shared venture where the light finally puts down roots.

sections.h2: The three cards of the 9-21-3 tail: what each means for a couple

head: Point
Arcanum
How it is derived
rows: 6 + 3: entries of the partners' personal tails
8 + 13 or 7 + 14: middles of the personal tails

paragraphs: The couple's karmic tail is not the personal tail of either partner. Each of its points is the sum of the matching points in two personal matrices. It is read from its main point: **D, the "Main task"** — where the couple stumbles and what it has to learn; this point is read mostly through its minus. **M, the "Entry to the task"** — the couple's shared wish, its agreements and its "common language"; with this wish the couple enters the task, and the same wish can turn into resistance. **N, the "Middle of the task"**, in our reading — how the couple lives the road from the wish to the task.

Put into one sentence: **the couple wants solitude for two, lives it as a road across the whole world, and has to learn home** — a place where its light becomes a visible harvest rather than a secret under a coat.

sections.h2: The first clue: "Have you got your lantern?"
paragraphs: In 1888 Stevenson published an essay, "The Lantern-Bearers", about a boys' game from his childhood in a fishing town on the Scottish coast. Towards the end of September, when the nights were already black, the boys bought tin bull's-eye lanterns, buckled them to their belts and buttoned their top-coats over them. There was one rule: keep the light inside. When two of them met in the dark there would be an anxious "Have you got your lantern?" and a gratified "Yes!"

Then comes about the most precise description of The Hermit to be found outside a deck: "The essence of this bliss was to walk by yourself in the black night; the slide shut, the top-coat buttoned; not a ray escaping, whether to conduct your footsteps or to make your glory public: a mere pillar of darkness in the dark; and all the while, deep down in the privacy of your fool's heart, to know you had a bull's-eye at your belt, and to exult and sing over the knowledge." And the conclusion the essay was written for: **"To one who has not the secret of the lanterns, the scene upon the links is meaningless."** From outside — wet, cold boys. From inside — heaven.

This is the entry to the task for a 9-21-3 couple. Its common language is that password. The two recognise each other by a light that cannot be seen from outside. They need no audience: an evening in one room, each busy with something of their own, is not a quarrel for them but the best kind of closeness. They have their own words, their own jokes, their own pace. They tell others about important things after the fact, once everything is decided.

Stevenson wrote down the wish itself ten years before the essay. In the autumn of 1878 he walked alone for twelve days through the Cévennes with a donkey called Modestine — by most accounts to put distance between himself and a love his friends and family disapproved of: Fanny had gone back to her husband in California. One night he slept under the pines, "between four and five thousand feet towards the stars", and wrote: "And yet even while I was exulting in my solitude I became aware of a strange lack. I wished a companion to lie near me in the starlight, silent and not moving, but ever within touch. For there is a fellowship more quiet even than solitude, and which, rightly understood, is **solitude made perfect**. And to live out of doors with the woman a man loves is of all lives the most complete and free."
That sentence holds the whole entry of the tail: not loneliness but solitude for two. And its last words already show the next card: "complete" — and Wen names the theme of The World as completion.

**Where the entry becomes resistance.** Point M stands on the line of tasks, so the same wish can work against the couple. A lantern under a coat keeps you warm, but it does not shine outward. From outside the couple looks cold and strange, and friends say "you've vanished". Inside, the unsaid piles up: each withdraws into a shell, hurt is lived through in silence, the conversation is put off, because silence counts as normal between them. Twenty years after her husband's death Fanny wrote in the preface to her diary: "Contrary to the general idea, my husband was a man of few intimate friends, and even with these he was reticent to a degree." And she admitted she had cut from the diary things pertaining to the private affairs of other persons, "and, naturally, our own". The lamp stayed under the coat.
In Waite's divinatory list, The World carries words that read like this couple's biography: "Assured success, recompense, voyage, route, emigration, flight, change of place."

In the summer of 1879 Fanny cabled Stevenson that she was leaving her husband, and in August he set off to join her without telling his parents. He sailed from Glasgow in the second cabin of the steamer Devonia, then crossed the whole of America on an emigrant train. Both parts of his account of that journey — the sea part, "From the Clyde to Sandy Hook", and the land part, "Across the Plains", published together as The Amateur Emigrant — can be read to the end without a single mention of the woman he was travelling to. He explains his choice of cabin by saying he was "anxious to see the worst of emigrant life" and "had some work to finish on the voyage". A whole ocean and a continent crossed — and the lantern still under the coat.

They married in May 1880 in San Francisco: she was forty, he was twenty-nine. They spent the honeymoon in an abandoned bunkhouse of the Silverado mine on the slope of Mount Saint Helena, high above the valley, and Stevenson named all four of them — himself, his wife, her son and the dog — "the King and Queen of Silverado", "the Crown Prince" and "the Grand Duke". Then came Davos, Hyères, Bournemouth and Saranac Lake in America. In June 1888 the family chartered the yacht Casco and sailed out of San Francisco into the Pacific: the Marquesas, Tahiti, Hawaii, then the schooner Equator, then the steamer Janet Nichol. Samoans gave Fanny the name Aolele — "flying cloud". Of the Janet Nichol cruise she would write: "perhaps the happiest period of my life".

This is the middle of the tail — **how the couple lives its road**. For a 9-21-3 couple shared solitude does not stay put: it moves house. Two such people change cities and countries easily, build a life out of different cultures, truly get to know each other on the road, and after time apart miss each other all the more. The World is their joint project: a shared philosophy, a shared map, a shared habit of looking far ahead.

But the card has a reverse side, and Stevenson wrote it down himself. On the schooner Equator he began a poem, "To My Wife", about how long it would be before she saw again a woodland lane with bramble and brier and the wayside smoke over the huts. Here instead, he writes, "from the sea the unfruitful sun shall rise", the allotted hours shall wheel in vain, and the sun shall plunge again "in the unpregnant ocean", while she has to live in the "most unwomanly bower / Of the wild-swerving cabin". The poem remained a fragment and breaks off mid-line. **The World gave this couple breadth, but not what only The Empress can give — fruit.**

The second reverse side is when the world for two closes into a wreath. The couple lives by its own rules and outsiders are not admitted; one quietly remakes the other to fit their own worldview; the days repeat like Groundhog Day; there are more secrets than conversations. Sometimes it is an endless cycle of splitting up and getting back together, where every departure is passed off as freedom. Waite's World reversed reads "Inertia, fixity, stagnation, permanence." For a couple whose middle is a road, stopping means risking stagnation. That is why home is the hardest thing for it.

sections.h2: The third clue: "My house, I say"
paragraphs: The house Stevenson called "mine" was a gift. In 1885 the writer's father, Thomas Stevenson, bought a villa in Bournemouth as a wedding present for Fanny. The son had chosen its new name before they moved in. "I am now a beastly householder," he wrote to his friend Edmund Gosse on 12 March 1885. "I shall call my house Skerryvore when I get it." Skerryvore is a lighthouse on a reef off the Scottish island of Tiree, built in 1844 by his uncle Alan. Underwoods contains a poem about the house: "For love of lovely words, and for the sake / Of those, my kinsmen and my countrymen, / Who early and late in the windy ocean toiled / **To plant a star for seamen**, where was then / The surfy haunt of seals and cormorants: / I, on the lintel of this cot, inscribe / The name of a strong tower."

A lighthouse's name above the door of a home is the whole 9-21-3 tail in one gesture. **The Hermit stands at the entrance to The Empress.** The couple still lives under the sign of its lantern, while the house is already waiting for someone to start living in it.

In the same collection, right after the Skerryvore poems, there are twelve lines that hold this card's lesson. "My house, I say. But hark to the sunny doves / That make my roof the arena of their loves… Our house, they say; and mine, the cat declares…" My house and our house — that is the whole difference between The Hermit and The Empress.
The couple's main task is read through what does not work, and here the story offers a scene for every minus.

**A house that was a gift.** The Empress as a task tests whether the couple can stand on its own ground: step out from under the family's wing, live on its own money, make decisions without looking to the elders. Skerryvore was a gift from his father, and until the success of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde in 1886, according to biographers, the household's main income was a paternal allowance of £250 a year. Thomas Stevenson's fortune had been made building lighthouses: the house with a lighthouse's name lived on lighthouse money.

**A house that rests on one person.** In The Silverado Squatters Stevenson describes his day at the mine honestly and almost cheerfully: in the morning he made porridge and coffee, drew water and prepared the kindling — and that ended his domestic duties. "Thenceforth my wife laboured single-handed in the palace, and I lay or wandered on the platform at my own sweet will." A home where comfort is made by one person is also a minus of The Empress, even when it is laughed about.

**A house that eats the work.** In January 1890 the Stevensons bought 314 acres of forest on the slope of Mount Vaea on the island of Upolu and built the islands' first two-storey house there. Fanny managed the estate and worked on it herself. In November 1890 Stevenson wrote to a friend: "Our place is in a deep cleft of Vaea Mountain, some six hundred feet above the sea, embowered in forest, which is our strangling enemy, and which we combat with axes and dollars. I went crazy over outdoor work, and had at last to confine myself to the house, or literature must have gone by the board." And then the formula of the whole conflict: **"If I go out and make sixpence, bossing my labourers and plying the cutlass or the spade, idiot conscience applauds me; if I sit in the house and make twenty pounds, idiot conscience wails over my neglect and the day wasted."** The garden against the writing desk, The Empress against The Hermit — inside one person.

The same letters hold a scene of The Empress at her best. His wife had bread to bake, but between whiles she came down to weed the prickly sensitive plant in the paddock with him. And at night, as soon as he shut his eyes, he saw "endless vivid deeps of grass and weed, each plant particular and distinct" — "a phenomenon to which both Fanny and I are quite accustomed". Two people who see the same garden when they close their eyes — that is "our house". The couple had a harvest of another kind too: Stevenson recalled how he and his wife planned a joint volume of stories, for which she wrote "The Shadow on the Bed"; in 1885 their joint book The Dynamiter came out, and Lloyd, Fanny's son, later wrote three novels with his stepfather.

Wen describes the reversed Empress as effort that yields no result: "There is a sense of emptiness and no production after much work and effort." This is the main risk for a 9-21-3 couple. It invests a great deal — in travel, in conversation, in its own world — but neither the couple nor the people around it can see the fruit. What it has to learn is not love — love sits at its centre — but how to make love bear a harvest.

sections.h2: Lighthouse and house: what Waite wrote about these cards
paragraphs: This section is about the images of the Waite deck and his text; the cards on our site are drawn differently.

**The Hermit.** Waite notes that his card differs from the conventional models in one thing only: "the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer". "It is a star which shines in the lantern", and The Hermit is "holding up his beacon on an eminence". The boys in Stevenson's essay hid their lanterns completely; Waite uncovered his. For a couple this is a direction of travel: from a light under a coat to a light by which others can see where to go. Stevenson, son and grandson of lighthouse builders, has the same pair of images in his two Skerryvore poems: his kinsmen toiled "to plant a star for seamen", and in "Skerryvore: The Parallel" he sets his sunny house of brick and pine, where "the truant gull / Skims the green level of the lawn, his wing / Dispetals roses", beside a granite tower that stands in the sweep of winds, "Immovable, immortal, eminent." The last word, eminent, shares its root with eminence — the height on which Waite places his Hermit. House and lighthouse are the two halves of one parallel, the M and D of this tail.

**The Empress.** In Waite's description "a field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water", and **"the sceptre which she bears is surmounted by the globe of this world"**. The World the couple travelled through in the middle of the tail becomes, in The Empress's hand, a small globe. A home does not cancel the road — it takes the world into its palm. Waite's divinatory list for The Empress begins "Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days". Set beside The World reversed ("Inertia, fixity, stagnation") this answers the couple's main fear: for Waite, home is not immobility but action.

**The World and The Lovers.** For Waite The World is "the perfection and end of the Cosmos, the secret which is within it". The Lovers, the atmosphere of every such couple, read in his list as "Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome."

Wen has a clue of her own. She assigns all three cards of the tail the same element, Earth, and notes that yin energy is dominant in each. She reads The Hermit's lantern both as light for others and as the sign of "someone who sees the world through his or her own light" — a ready-made bridge from 9 to 21. And of the reversed Empress she writes that "the element of Earth is missing and is the cause of imbalance" and of lack of results. A tail standing wholly on Earth, in a couple that lives on the road, is an exact portrait of the task: come down to earth.

sections.h2: Where the 9-21-3 tail comes from: the numbers as evidence
paragraphs: **Rarity.** This tail occurs in roughly one couple in 4,389 — 95th place out of the 97 possible couple tails.

**Two partners, two doors.** The 9-21-3 tail comes from only two combinations of personal tails: 3-13-10 with 6-8-20 (70% of such couples) or 3-7-22 with 6-14-8 (30%). In both cases one partner's personal tail begins with The Empress (3) and the other's with The Lovers (6). The couple's entry is their sum: 6 + 3 = 9. **This couple's solitude is made of love and home.** There is no point asking which of the two is "responsible" for the home: the couple's points mean something different from personal ones, and the task belongs to both.

**An atmosphere made from the road.** At the centre of the chart every such couple has The Lovers, 6 — in 100% of cases. The same six comes from the middle plus the main task, 21 + 3 = 24 → 6, and from the whole tail, 9 + 21 + 3 = 33 → 6. Our reading: this couple's love is what you get when the road and the home are added together.

**A middle no single person has.** In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: 9 + 3 would give 12, The Hanged Man. In a couple the middle is added up from the partners' middles, and it comes out as 21 — the same digits reversed. That is why 9-21-3 never occurs as a personal tail. Where one person with these ends would hang in a pause, the couple goes out into the world.

**The couple's values.** In the sphere "The couple's values", 84.9% of such couples have The Moon and 15.1% The Hermit. The Moon is night, dreams and imagination, and for the Stevensons it too worked for the shared home: in "A Chapter on Dreams" he says the plot of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde came to him in a dream after "one of those financial fluctuations". Lisovskaya advises Moon couples to accept a partner's occasional need to withdraw as a way of recovering, not as a lack of love — and for a tail that begins with The Hermit this is especially apt.

**The tail made of the same numbers.** A couple can also have 9-3-21 — almost 15 times more often (0.339% of couples). There The Empress is in the middle and The World is the main task: first home, then going out into the world. The atmosphere differs too: at the centre 89.6% of those couples have The Devil, and only 10.4% The Lovers.

Take two people born on 7 August 1976 and 4 January 1976. The first has the personal tail 6-8-20 and a centre of 4. The second has 3-13-10 and a centre of 20. The couple's points are added pairwise, and a sum above 22 is reduced by adding its digits.

In "The couple's values" these two have The Moon, 18 — like most couples with this tail. This is the first of the two combinations: The Empress opens the personal tail of the person born on 4 January 1976, The Lovers open that of the person born on 7 August 1976, and their sum opens the couple's tail.
The shadow of this tail runs in a circle, and there is no villain in it — only a habit of hiding the light.

First the couple finds a refuge in each other: nobody else is needed, evenings for two beat any company. Then the refuge starts to move: new cities, trips, projects, relocations — or the opposite, a closed world with its own rules. Every movement feels like life, and any stop feels like stagnation. Years pass, and one day it turns out that a great deal has been invested and there is nothing to show: no home that has become "ours", no venture that has grown, no circle of people who know these two. The couple carries its dissatisfaction back into its shell, and the lantern is buttoned under the coat again.
The way out of the circle is not to love solitude less, nor to stop travelling. The way out is The Empress: to give what the couple already has some soil and a harvest.

ul: **Open the lantern at least a hand's width.** Say out loud what exactly makes their "two of us" so precious, and let two or three people into their world.
**Give the road a home port.** Travel from home, not instead of home: a place to come back to is not a defeat of freedom.
**Make "ours" visible.** A garden, a shared venture, a tradition, a book, a house the couple fits out with its own hands — something that grows and can be shown.
**Share the home fairly.** Comfort that rests on one person is a minus of The Empress, even if it is joked about.
**Stand on your own ground.** Your own money, your own decisions, a calling of one's own for each partner — not only a shared one.

sections.h2: "Home is the sailor, home from sea"
paragraphs: Stevenson wrote down the strong version of this tail too — in "Requiem", from the same Underwoods. Its last lines run: "Home is the sailor, home from sea, / And the hunter home from the hill." The hill is The Hermit's height. The sea is The World's road. Home is The Empress. The three cards of the tail stand in two lines, and all three converge on one word.

This couple had two answers to the question of happiness. His, in a letter from Vailima: "I was only happy once; that was at Hyères." The house at Hyères was called La Solitude; that name dates his poem "To a Gardener", in which he asks for onions, artichokes and asparagus to be grown for his supper and promises himself "A book, a taper, and a cup / Of country wine". Hers, about the voyage on the Janet Nichol: "perhaps the happiest period of my life". He was happy in solitude with a garden, she on the road. Vailima became an attempt to fit both kinds of happiness under one roof: a house on a mountain above the sea where two people weed together.

The story has a small rhyme as well. On the night under the pines in the Cévennes Stevenson woke thirsty and drank the water from his tin. The name Vailima means "water in the hand" in Samoan: in an old tale a woman brought water in her hand to a thirsty companion. The popular rendering "five waters" is considered a mistake: the word lima means both "hand" and "five".

And the whole tail once fitted into a single rainy day. In the summer of 1881 at Braemar in Scotland, kept indoors between four walls by the weather, Stevenson was painting in watercolours with a schoolboy, Fanny's son, and drew the map of an island. He labelled it "Treasure Island". Solitude between four walls, a whole world on a sheet of paper, a family in which a book is growing — 9, 21 and 3 at one table. **A couple with this tail is strong when its lantern does not hide from the world and the world does not lead it away from home.**

intro: The riddle of this tail is written into its numbers. In a personal destiny matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its two ends. Here it is the other way round: the end is made from the road. 9 + 21 = 30, and 3 + 0 = 3. **The Hermit who has travelled through The World adds up to The Empress.** The main task does not fall on the couple from outside — it grows out of the way these two live.

Someone once lived this arithmetic for real. In the spring of 1885 Robert Louis Stevenson, the author of Treasure Island, moved with his wife into a house his father had given to Fanny — and gave it the name of a lighthouse. Behind that gesture lies the whole story of Stevenson and Fanny Osbourne: a night in the mountains when he longed for a companion "ever within touch", an emigrant steamer, a shack in an abandoned mine, three vessels in the Pacific and, at last, Vailima on Samoa — a house, a garden and a large family. None of this proves the Stevensons had this exact tail: their dates are not calculated here. It is a plot in which the three cards read as one story.

faq.q: What does the 9-21-3 karmic tail mean in compatibility?
faq.a: It is a couple's tail with three cards: The Hermit at the entry to the task, The World in the middle and The Empress as the main task. The couple wants solitude for two and a quiet language of its own, lives it as a shared road across the world, and has to learn home — to make its union visible and fruitful: a shared household, a venture of its own, its own ground.

In the order of the middle and the main task. In 9-21-3 the couple first goes out into the world, and the task is home; in 9-3-21 it first builds a home, and the task is to go out into the world. 9-3-21 occurs almost 15 times more often, and those couples most often have The Devil at the centre, while 9-21-3 couples always have The Lovers.

faq.q: Why does this tail never appear in a personal matrix?
faq.a: In a personal matrix the middle of the tail is the sum of its ends: with an entry of 9 and a task of 3 it would be 12. In a couple the middle is added up from the two partners' middles, which gives 21. Such a middle exists only in a couple.

faq.q: Is this a bad tail for a couple?
faq.a: No. A tail passes no verdicts and predicts nothing: it shows which task the couple will find most interesting and most difficult. In 9-21-3 the atmosphere is always The Lovers, and the main task is learning to turn love and solitude into a home that grows.

faq.q: How can a couple find out whether it has this tail?
faq.a: Calculate compatibility from the two birth dates. The couple's entry to the task is the sum of the entries of the personal tails, the middle is the sum of the middles, and the main task is the sum of the main tasks; if a sum is above 22, its digits are added together. For 9-21-3 one partner's personal tail begins with 3 and the other's with 6.

report: Waite notes that his Hermit's lamp, unlike on the older cards, is not covered by the mantle, and that his Empress holds a sceptre "surmounted by the globe of this world". The strong version of the tail is both at once: the light no longer hides under a coat, and the world travelled together fits in the hand, at home. Stevenson put it into two lines of "Requiem": **"Home is the sailor, home from sea, / And the hunter home from the hill."** The hill is The Hermit, the sea is The World, home is The Empress.
